holidays.name: National Hangover Day
holidays.description: The morning-after holiday for anyone who rang in the new year a little too enthusiastically. Expect water, greasy breakfasts, sunglasses indoors, and a slow start to the year.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance of unclear origin. It follows naturally from New Year's Eve celebrations.
holidays.funFact: Hangover remedies go back thousands of years. Ancient Romans were said to turn to fried canaries, and some Victorians relied on a pick-me-up called a prairie oyster, made from a raw egg.

holidays.name: National Bloody Mary Day
holidays.description: A salute to the brunch classic of tomato juice, vodka, and spices, often topped with celery, olives, bacon, or even a tiny cheeseburger. It's a cocktail that doubles as a garnish buffet.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance of unclear origin. It's linked to New Year's Day because the drink has long been a hangover remedy.
holidays.funFact: Bartender Fernand Petiot is often credited with the drink's modern form, which he mixed at the St. Regis hotel in New York in the 1930s.

holidays.name: Polar Bear Plunge Day
holidays.description: Brave swimmers start the year by running into icy lake or ocean water, often in costumes. The plunge is fast, cold, and loud, and usually ends with a dash for a towel and hot chocolate.
holidays.origin: New Year's Day polar bear plunges have been a tradition for over a century. The Vancouver Polar Bear Swim began in 1920 and the Coney Island Polar Bear Club was founded in 1903.
holidays.funFact: Vancouver's English Bay swim draws thousands of participants every year, making it one of the largest in the world.
